bib.title: Introduction to Machine Learning with Python, Chapter 2: Supervised Learning

question: Which supervised learning algorithms exist, how does each control model complexity, and when should each be used?
contributions: Walk through k-NN, linear models, naive Bayes, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, kernel SVMs and MLPs with scikit-learn on small datasets
Show uncertainty estimates via decision_function and predict_proba

limits: Single train/test split per experiment, no cross-validation, no confidence intervals; differences of ~0.01 accuracy on 143 test points (Breast Cancer) are a few samples. Footnote 12 notes several models make exactly the same four mistakes.
Parameter tuning is done by eye on the test set (e.g. alpha, C chosen by looking at test scores); the chapter defers proper tuning to Chapter 6.

Dated API: load_boston (removed from scikit-learn 1.2), MLPClassifier(algorithm=...) now solver=..., LogisticRegression penalty='l1' needs solver liblinear/saga now, GradientBoosting defaults, RBF gamma default now 'scale', Axes3D usage, Python 2/3-era print formatting.

Dated advice: 'xgboost ... at the time of writing is faster' (scikit-learn now has HistGradientBoosting; LightGBM and CatBoost exist); neural networks section recommends keras/lasagna/theano/tensorflow; 'deep learning has recently seen a revival'; tree-based models preferred over SVMs 'these days' is still broadly true for tabular data.
Boston Housing dataset is ethically problematic and removed from scikit-learn.
Small and synthetic datasets (26-569 points); intuition from low-dimensional data may not transfer, as the authors concede.

Typos in text: Gaussian kernel written exp(gamma||x1-x2||^2) without minus sign; 'LinearLogistic'; 'BinaryNB'; 'Fig 2-12 alpha=0.00001' vs code 0.0001; hidden-unit formula repeats the same weights w[.,0] for h[0], h[1], h[2].
practices: Start with a simple model (linear, naive Bayes or nearest neighbours) before complex ones (p.128).
Choose the simplest model that fits; model complexity should match the variety in the data; more data beats tuning (pp.28-29).
k-NN: scale/preprocess data; use as a baseline; poor on hundreds of features or sparse data; try 3 or 5 neighbours and tune (p.44).
Search alpha and C on a logarithmic scale (p.67).
Default to L2 (ridge); use L1 when few features matter or interpretability is needed; ElasticNet combines both (pp.55, 67).
Do not read linear-model coefficient signs as class association, especially with correlated features (p.60, p.67).
For very large data use solver='sag', SGDClassifier or SGDRegressor (p.67).
Naive Bayes: great baseline for very large high-dimensional/sparse count data; MultinomialNB usually beats BernoulliNB on large documents (p.70).
Decision trees: pick one pre-pruning parameter (max_depth, max_leaf_nodes or min_samples_leaf) to prevent overfitting; no scaling needed (pp.82-83).
Trees cannot extrapolate beyond the training range; do not use for trending forecasts without care (p.82).
Random forests: first try defaults; more trees always better; max_features default sqrt(n_features) classification, log2(n_features) regression; set random_state; n_jobs=-1 (pp.87-88).

Gradient boosting: fix n_estimators from time/memory budget, then search learning_rate; keep max_depth at five or less; try random forest first, move to GBM for last accuracy or faster prediction (pp.89-92).
Kernel SVM: scale all features to a similar range (e.g. 0-1), tune C and gamma together; practical up to ~10,000 samples, hard at 100,000 (pp.102-104).
Neural networks: standardise inputs to mean 0 variance 1; start with one or two hidden layers; first build a network big enough to overfit, then shrink or raise alpha; use adam or l-bfgs (p.118).
Check classifier uncertainty with decision_function / predict_proba; use classes_ to map back to labels (pp.120-127).
Compute scaling statistics on the training set only and apply the same transform to the test set (p.103).

terms.definition: Building a model too complex for the information available, fitting the particularities of the training set so that it fails to generalise.
Choosing too simple a model, which does badly even on the training set.
Explicitly restricting a model to avoid overfitting.
Penalises the sum of absolute coefficient values; some coefficients become exactly zero (lasso).
Penalises the Euclidean length of the coefficient vector (ridge); default in LogisticRegression and LinearSVC.
Stopping tree growth early (max depth, max leaves, min samples per node).
Draw n_samples points at random with replacement from n_samples data points.
Each tree gives class probabilities; they are averaged and the highest wins.
A simple model, such as a shallow tree, combined with many others in gradient boosting.
Learn a classifier in a higher-dimensional space by computing scalar products of the expanded representation directly, without computing the expansion.
The subset of training points on the border between classes that define the SVM decision boundary.
Reported uncertainty matches correctness: predictions made with 70% certainty are correct 70% of the time.
Plot of model performance as a function of dataset size.

min_on_training = X_train.min(axis=0)
range_on_training = (X_train - min_on_training).max(axis=0)
X_train_scaled = (X_train - min_on_training) / range_on_training
X_test_scaled = (X_test - min_on_training) / range_on_training

mean_on_train = X_train.mean(axis=0)
std_on_train = X_train.std(axis=0)
X_train_scaled = (X_train - mean_on_train) / std_on_train
X_test_scaled = (X_test - mean_on_train) / std_on_train
